# Immune thrombocytopenia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Platelet and coagulation disorders > Immune thrombocytopenia*

[Original Article Link](/library/8q0OZh)

---

## Summary

Immune <u>thrombocytopenia</u> (ITP) is a type of <u>thrombocytopenia</u> involving the formation of <u>autoantibodies</u> against <u>platelets</u>. ITP may be a primary disease or occur secondary to a known trigger (e.g., <u>SLE</u>, <u>HIV</u>, <u>hepatitis C</u>, medications). It is commonly seen in children as a <u>self-limiting</u> illness following a viral infection, and in adults as a chronic illness. Most patients are asymptomatic, however, patients may occasionally present with minor mucocutaneous bleeding (e.g., <u>petechiae</u>, <u>purpura</u>, <u>epistaxis</u>) or, rarely, with severe bleeding (e.g., gastrointestinal or <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u>). Treatment recommendations vary depending on the presence and severity of symptoms. First-line medical therapy consists of <u>corticosteroids</u>, IVIG, or <u>anti-D immunoglobulin</u>, and is indicated for patients with non-life-threatening symptoms affecting their quality-of-life, and for adults with little-to-no symptoms and <u>platelet counts</u> below 30,000/mmÂ³. Children with little-to-no symptoms can typically be managed with observation alone regardless of <u>platelet count</u>. Second-line treatments (i.e., <u>thrombopoietin receptor agonists</u>, <u>rituximab</u>, <u>splenectomy</u>) may be required for refractory, persistent or chronic cases. Patients with life-threatening hemorrhage, neurological symptoms, or those requiring urgent surgical interventions should receive immediate combination medical therapy (i.e., <u>corticosteroids</u> plus IVIG) along with <u>platelet transfusions</u> and <u>hemostatic control</u> interventions when necessary.




See also “<u>Thrombocytopenia</u>.”

---

## Definitions

Immune <u>thrombocytopenia</u> has previously been referred to as <u>idiopathic</u> <u>thrombocytopenic</u> <u>purpura</u>, however, this term is outdated.




* Primary immune thrombocytopenia: : an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated <u>thrombocytopenia</u> (< 100,000/mmÂ³) with no known precipitating cause [[2]](/library/BibzFt)

* Secondary immune thrombocytopenia: an autoimmune hematologic disorder causing isolated <u>thrombocytopenia</u> that is secondary to an identifiable trigger (see “Etiology”).

* Newly diagnosed ITP: all cases within the first 3 months of diagnosis  [[2]](/library/BibzFt)

* Persistent ITP: ITP lasting 3–12 months

* Chronic ITP: ITP lasting > 12 months

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: up to ∼ 10 per 100,000  [[3]](/library/1cX2YC)[[4]](/library/WcXPYC)

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> [[3]](/library/1cX2YC)

* Children

* Highest <u>prevalence</u> in children < 5 years of age [[3]](/library/1cX2YC)

* Typically <u>self-limiting</u> after a viral infection; 80% of cases resolve within 12 months [[5]](/library/TcX6bC)

* Adults

* Highest <u>prevalence</u> in individuals > 55 years of age [[3]](/library/1cX2YC)

* 80% of patients develop chronic ITP. [[5]](/library/TcX6bC)

* An incidental finding on a routine <u>CBC</u> in 25% of cases [[6]](/library/FVXgwC)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Primary ITP</u>: <u>idiopathic</u> (most common)  [[7]](/library/2cXTbC)

* <u>Secondary ITP</u> associated with:

* Autoimmune disorders: <u>SLE</u>, <u>antiphospholipid syndrome</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u>: <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>leukemia</u> (particularly <u>CLL</u>)

* Infection: <u>HIV</u>, <u>HCV</u>

* Drugs: e.g., <u>quinine</u>,;  <u>beta-lactam antibiotics</u>, <u>carbamazepine</u>, <u>heparin</u>, <u>vaccines</u>, <u>linezolid</u>, <u>sulfonamides</u>, <u>vancomycin</u>, <u>TMP-SMX</u>, <u>antiepileptics</u>  [[8]](/library/INXYcA)

---

## Pathophysiology

Antiplatelet <u>antibodies</u> (mostly <u>IgG</u> directed against, e.g., <u>GpIIb/IIIa</u>, <u>GpIb</u>/IX) bind to surface <u>proteins</u> on <u>platelets</u> → sequestration by <u>spleen</u> and <u>liver</u> → ↓ <u>platelet count</u> → <u>bone marrow</u> <u>megakaryocytes</u> and <u>platelet production</u> increase in response (in most cases)  [[9]](/library/3QbSDt)

---

## Clinical features

Clinical features can correlate with <u>platelet count</u> (see also “<u>Clinical features of thrombocytopenia</u>” and “<u>Clinical features of bleeding disorders</u>”).




* Most commonly

* Asymptomatic

* <u>Splenomegaly</u> is typically absent.  [[10]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Minor mucocutaneous bleeding (less common)

* Subcutaneous: e.g., <u>bruising</u>, <u>petechiae</u>, <u>purpura</u>

* <u>Mucosal</u>: e.g., mild <u>epistaxis</u>, gingival bleeding

* Other types of bleeding (rare)

* Gastrointestinal: e.g, <u>melena</u>

* Genitourinary: e.g., <u>hematuria</u>, <u>menorrhagia</u>

* <u>CNS</u>: e.g., features of <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u>

* Prolonged or excessive traumatic or surgical bleeding





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Splenomegaly</u> is very unusual in ITP and makes other diagnoses more likely!




> [!NOTE]
> There should be suspicion for ITP in a child with <u>thrombocytopenia</u> and <u>petechiae</u> following a viral illness!

## Diagnosis

ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion; patients typically have a <u>low platelet count</u> with no other abnormalities.  [[5]](/library/TcX6bC)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[10]](/library/kIYm1q)[[11]](/library/mL0Vyg)[[12]](/library/QcXuXC)




#### Routine




* <u>CBC</u>: ↓ <u>platelet count</u> (< 100,000/mmÂ³)

* <u>Coagulation panel</u>: usually normal

* <u>Bleeding time</u>: may be prolonged

* <u>Peripheral blood smear</u>: normal to large <u>platelets</u>  [[13]](/library/PcXWcC)





#### Additional investigations




* All adults: <u>HIV</u> and <u>HCV screening</u>

* <u>Bone marrow biopsy</u>

* Consider in atypical cases or if there is diagnostic uncertainty

* Findings: normal or ↑ <u>megakaryocytes</u> [[5]](/library/TcX6bC)

* Additional testing as required: consider in suspected <u>secondary ITP</u>, e.g., <u>antinuclear antibodies</u> in <u>SLE</u> or <u>H. pylori</u> testing if the patient has GI symptoms or is from a high <u>prevalence</u> area

## Treatment

### Approach




These recommendations are consistent with the 2019 American Society of <u>Hematology</u> ITP guidelines and the 2019 International Consensus Report on <u>primary ITP</u> investigation and management.  [[14]](/library/pRbLLt)[[15]](/library/KcXUWC)




| <br>Management approach for ITP [[14]](/library/pRbLLt)[[15]](/library/KcXUWC)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Management | Newly diagnosed ITP | Persistent or chronic ITP |
| All patients | <br><br>* Identify and treat underlying causes.<br><br>* Consider stopping medications that impair <u>platelet</u> function, e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>.   [[16]](/library/3dXSpC)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Patients requiring emergency treatment: <br><br>* Life-threatening bleeding<br><br>* Acute neurological features<br><br>* Anticipated urgent <u>surgery</u> or invasive procedure<br><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Attempt <u>hemostatic control</u> if bleeding is present.<br><br>* Start combination therapy:<br><br>* <u>Corticosteroids</u>: e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* PLUS <u>intravenous immunoglobulin</u> (IVIG)  DOSAGE<br><br>* PLUS <u>platelet transfusions</u> as needed for the management of acute bleeding  [[15]](/library/KcXUWC)[[17]](/library/5IXiWz)<br><br>* If no response, consider a <u>thrombopoietin</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>agonist</u> (<u>TPO-RA</u>), e.g., <u>romiplostim</u>  DOSAGE<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Patients with: <br><br>* No symptoms<br><br>* Only minor mucocutaneous bleeding<br><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Conservative management</u> preferred for:<br><br>* Adults with a <u>platelet count</u> â¥ 30,000/mmÂ³<br><br>* Children with any <u>platelet count</u><br><br>* First-line medical therapy: indicated for adults with <u>platelet count</u> < 30,000/mmÂ³<br><br><br> | <br>* Consider subsequent therapeutic options depending on individual patient factors.<br><br> |
| <br>Patients with: Significant non-life-threatening <u>mucosal</u> bleeding  Symptoms impacting quality-of-life<br> | <br><br>* First-line medical therapy<br><br>* Indicated for adults<br><br>* Can be considered in children<br><br>* Consider subsequent therapeutic options if refractory to first-line medical therapy.<br><br><br> |  |
| Disposition | <br><br>* Hospital admission should be considered for:<br><br>* Patients requiring emergency treatment<br><br>* Patients with significant functional impairment or risk of significant hemorrhage<br><br>* Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic adults with <u>platelet counts</u> < 20,000/mmÂ³<br><br>* Outpatient management with <u>hematology</u> follow-up is appropriate for:<br><br>* Patients receiving <u>conservative management</u><br><br>* Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic adults receiving first-line medical therapy and <u>platelet counts</u> 20–29,999 /mm³<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Can typically be managed as an outpatient, regardless of <u>platelet</u> level<br><br>* Consider hospital admission if significant functional impairment or need for emergency treatment.<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Patients that can be managed as outpatients should receive expedited <u>hematology</u> follow-up within 24–72 hours. [[14]](/library/pRbLLt)




### <u>Conservative management</u> [[14]](/library/pRbLLt)[[15]](/library/KcXUWC)




* Indications for observation

* Children: no symptoms or only mild mucocutaneous bleeding with any <u>platelet count</u>

* Adults: no symptoms or minor mucocutaneous bleeding with a <u>platelet count</u> of â¥ 30,000/mmÂ³

* All patients: Refer to <u>hematology</u> for regular monitoring and counseling on bleeding risks.





### First-line medical therapy [[14]](/library/pRbLLt)[[15]](/library/KcXUWC)




* Preferred: <u>Corticosteroids</u>  [[17]](/library/5IXiWz)

* <u>Dexamethasone</u> DOSAGE  [[14]](/library/pRbLLt)

* OR <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE  [[14]](/library/pRbLLt)[[15]](/library/KcXUWC)

* Alternatives: if contraindication, non-response, or intolerance to <u>corticosteroids</u> 

* <u>Intravenous immunoglobulin</u> (IVIG) DOSAGE

* OR <u>anti-Rho(D) immunoglobulin</u> DOSAGE 

* <u>FDA</u> black box warning: risk of <u>intravascular hemolysis</u>

* In-hospital monitoring: recommended for at least 8 hours after administration

* <u>Urinalysis</u> for <u>hematuria</u> and <u>hemoglobinuria</u> prior to therapy, and at 2 hours and 4 hours after administration.

* Order <u>hemolysis workup</u> in patients with characteristic clinical features (e.g., <u>back pain</u>, chills, urine discoloration)

* Side effects [[17]](/library/5IXiWz)

* IVIG: e.g., <u>thrombosis</u>, <u>aseptic meningitis</u>, infusion reactions

* <u>Anti-Rho(D) immunoglobulin</u>: e.g., <u>intravascular hemolysis</u> that can cause <u>anemia</u>, <u>multiorgan dysfunction</u>, <u>AKI</u>, <u>renal failure</u>, <u>DIC</u>, or <u>death</u>





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Anti-Rho(D) immunoglobulin</u> can cause potentially fatal <u>intravascular hemolysis</u> in patients with ITP. Close monitoring is recommended.




### Subsequent therapeutic options [[15]](/library/KcXUWC)




The following options should be considered in consultation with a specialist for patients with newly-diagnosed ITP refractory to first-line medical therapy, or persistent/chronic ITP.




* <u>Thrombopoietin receptor agonists</u> (<u>TPO-RAs</u>)

* <u>Romiplostim</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Eltrombopag</u> DOSAGE

* Avatrombopag DOSAGE

* <u>Rituximab</u> DOSAGE  [[2]](/library/BibzFt)

* <u>Splenectomy</u> 

* Indications

* Treatment-resistant <u>thrombocytopenia</u> lasting > 12 months

* Severe bleeding that does not respond to any other treatment

* Procedure: Minimally invasive <u>laparoscopic surgery</u> is preferred.

* Complications: See “<u>Asplenic sepsis</u>.”

* Prevention of complications: See “<u>Management of asplenic patients</u>.”
